summary: Makes the US Secure Hash Algorithm 1 conveniently available to the Internet community, with a description and sample code.

eli5.summary: It describes a recipe that turns any message into a short fingerprint.

questions: how long is a sha-1 digest
how does sha-1 pad a message
subtitle: The SHA-1 hash algorithm written out for the Internet community, with reference C code.

tldr.problem: The US government adopted SHA-1 in FIPS 180-1, but the Internet community lacked a convenient, openly available description and code for it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo restates the algorithm: pad the message to a multiple of 512 bits, process it in 512-bit blocks through 80 steps each, and output a 160-bit message digest. It adds a demonstration C implementation.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that makes no independent security claim, and it has been updated by RFC 4634 and RFC 6234.

today: RFC 3174 is an Informational memo and has been updated by RFC 4634 and RFC 6234. It was not obsoleted according to the metadata.

sections.title: What SHA-1 Does
sections.content:
This document specifies the Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (SHA-1) for computing a condensed representation of a message or data file. Given a message of any length less than 2^64 bits, it produces a 160-bit output called a message digest. A digest can be fed to a signature algorithm, which is often more efficient than signing the whole message.

The text calls SHA-1 secure because it is computationally infeasible to find a message that matches a given digest, or two different messages with the same digest. The RFC stresses that most of its text comes from FIPS 180-1, and the security assertions are made by the US Government, not by the authors. Only the C code is original.
sections.eli5: SHA-1 squeezes a message of any size into a small fingerprint. If even one letter changes, the fingerprint almost surely looks completely different.

sections.title: Words, Blocks and Operations
sections.content:
SHA-1 works on 32-bit words, each written as 8 hex digits, and on blocks of 512 bits, which are 16 words. Integers from 0 to 2^32 - 1 are stored as words.

The algorithm uses bitwise AND, OR, XOR and NOT, addition of words modulo 2^32, and the circular left shift S^n(X), which rotates a word left by n positions for 0 <= n < 32.
sections.eli5: Think of Lego bricks of one fixed size. SHA-1 snaps them together and spins them around in set ways.

sections.title: Message Padding
sections.content:
SHA-1 processes 512-bit blocks, so the message is padded to make its total length a multiple of 512. A "1" bit is appended, then enough "0" bits so that the last 64 bits of the final block are free, and then the original message length in bits is written as a 64-bit integer (two words) into those last 64 bits.

The RFC's worked example pads the five-byte message "abcde" (40 bits). After the "1" there are 407 zero bits, and the final two words are 00000000 00000028, which is 40 in hex.
sections.eli5: Before packing a box, you fill the empty space with a standard filler and write the item count on the lid, so every box is the same size.

sections.title: Functions, Constants and the Digest
sections.content:
Eighty logical functions f(0) to f(79) and eighty constants K(0) to K(79) are used, split into four groups of 20 steps. The constants in hex are 5A827999, 6ED9EBA1, 8F1BBCDC and CA62C1D6.

Five word registers H0 to H4 start with fixed values (67452301, EFCDAB89, 98BADCFE, 10325476, C3D2E1F0). Each block is expanded into an 80-word sequence W(0) to W(79), then run through 80 steps that update the working words A to E. After each block, A to E are added into H0 to H4. After the last block, the digest is the 160-bit string H0 H1 H2 H3 H4.

A second method uses a 16-word circular queue instead of an 80-word array. It saves sixty-four 32-bit words of storage but is likely to run slower, and it gives the same digest.
sections.eli5: It is a big mixing machine. Every chunk of the message gets stirred into five numbers, and the final five numbers are the fingerprint.

sections.title: The C Reference Code
sections.content:
Section 7 gives a demonstration C implementation in three parts: a header (sha1.h), the code (sha1.c) and a test driver. The API is three calls: SHA1Reset, SHA1Input and SHA1Result. The hash size constant is 20 bytes.

The code works only on messages whose length is a multiple of 8 bits, and it needs 32-bit and 8-bit unsigned integer types. Its style follows the earlier MD4 and MD5 RFCs.
sections.eli5: Along with the recipe, the authors include a ready-made kitchen tool, written in the C programming language, that follows the recipe exactly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document is meant to give convenient open source access to the US Federal Information Processing Standard hash function SHA-1. It states that no independent assertion of the security of the function, for any particular use, is made by the authors.
sections.eli5: The authors copied the recipe but do not promise how strong the lock it makes is. That promise belongs to the people who invented it.
